speaker: Dhritarashtra
sanskrit: धृतराष्ट्र उवाच | धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः | मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय
english: Dhritarashtra said What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together eager for battle on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya.
brief_explanation: The holy plain, Kurukshetra, is named so because it belongs to the Kurus. Sanjaya, being impartial, is assembled there with those desirous to fight, including my people (Pandavas) and others. What did they do there?

speaker: Sanjaya
sanskrit: सञ्जय उवाच | दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा | आचार्यमुपसंगम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्
english: . Sanjaya said Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle-array, King Duryodhana then approached his teacher (Drona) and spoke these words.
brief_explanation: Duryodhana, upon seeing the army of the Pandavas drawn up for battle, approached his teacher and then spoke to King Dhritarashtra about it. (No additional commentary provided.)

sanskrit: पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम् | व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता
english: . "Behold, O Teacher! this mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.
brief_explanation: The teacher beholds the great army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed, led by Drupada's son, who is one of his disciples, demonstrating wisdom.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि | युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः
english: . Here are heroes, mighty archers, eal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yoyudhana (Satyaki), Virata and Drupada, of the great car (mighty warriors).
brief_explanation: Maharatha refers to a skilled warrior who can single-handedly fight against ten thousand archers. In this context, Yuyudhana, Virata, Drupada, Bhima, and Arjuna are the mighty heroes mentioned in the battle.

english: . "Dhrishtaketu, chekitana and the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit and Kuntibhoja and Saibya, the best men.
brief_explanation: These individuals mentioned are notable characters from ancient India: 1. Dhrishtaketu, a prince known for his wisdom. 2.

english: . "The strong Yodhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of great chariots (great heroes).
brief_explanation: Yudhamanyu, Vikranta, Uttamaujas, the strong, Saupta (son of Subhadra), Draupadeyas (sons of Draupadi) and all the Maharathas (great warriors) mentioned are significant figures in the Kurukshetra war.

english: . "Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to thee for thy information.
brief_explanation: The text refers to Arjuna asking if he should know about the best warriors among us and also among the twicorn ones, who are leaders in my army, for information purposes. Then Krishna responds that he will speak to Arjuna about them.

english: . "Thyself and Bhishma, and Karna and also Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and also Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta.

brief_explanation: Heroes who are ready to give up their lives, armed with various weapons and missiles, all skilled in battle for the sake of others.

brief_explanation: The verse suggests a comparison between our army, which is marshalled by Bhishma, and their army, which is marshalled by Bhima. Some interpret 'aparyaptam' as insufficient for our side, while others take it to mean unlimited for theirs.

english: . "Therefore do ye all, stationed in your respective positions, in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone."
brief_explanation: Protect Bhishma alone according to division in the armies, being stationed, all of you indeed, even in all places. (No commentary provided.)

The phrase "aparajita" indicates that these warriors were unconquered.

In this verse from the Gita, they blow conches separately, signaling the start of the battle.

brief_explanation: The context describes Arjuna, looking at Dhritarashtra's party and the monkey-signed soldiers preparing for battle, about to discharge weapons. He takes up his bow, addressing Hrishikesha (a name for Vishnu) as the Lord of the Earth, saying these words then.

sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत
english: Arjuna said In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot, O krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.
brief_explanation: In the middle of both armies, Krishna places His chariot and observes the armies while they are standing, desirous to fight. He beholds these troops with whom fighting must be done on this eve of battle. (1.21-1.22)

brief_explanation: In the middle of both armies, Krishna as Achyuta places his car and watches while he, along with those desirous to fight and standing, must be fought by him on the eve of battle.

sanskrit: कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः | धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत
english: . In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety, indeed, overcomes the whole family.
brief_explanation: The destruction of a family leads to the perishing of its immemorial religious rites, which are an integral part of spirituality. When the whole family is destroyed, impiety prevails, indicating the decline of Dharma.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः | स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः
english: . By the prevalence of impiety, O Krishna, the women of the family become corrupt; and , women being corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), there arises intermingling of castes.
brief_explanation: Krishna explains that the prevalence of impiety leads to the corruption of women, especially those in families, and among corrupt women, a caste mixture arises (Varshneya refers to the Brahmin caste).

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: सङ्करो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च | पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः
english: . Confusion of castes leads to hell the slayers of the family, for their forefathers fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-ball and water (libations).
brief_explanation: The term "Sankarah" denotes confusion of castes. For those who are slayers of family members, they fall into hell (narakaya) and their forefathers suffer due to their actions as they are deprived of the ritual offerings of rice and water (luptapindodakakriya).

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसङ्करकारकैः | उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः
english: . By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and the family are destroyed.
brief_explanation: The text suggests that those who commit evil deeds, specifically family destroyers causing intermingling of castes, will have their eternal caste and family religious rites destroyed. No explicit commentary is provided in the passage.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन | नरके नियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम (or नरकेऽनियतं)
english: . We have heard, O Janardana, that inevitable is the dwelling for an unknown period in hell for those men in whose families the religious practices have been destroyed.
brief_explanation: The Sivananda commentary does not provide a specific explanation for verse 1.44. However, the verse seems to suggest that those whose religious practices are destroyed dwell in hell for an unknown period, as it is stated: "Utsannakuladharmaanam manushyanam janardane narake aniyatam vasati iti anushushrurum" (We have heard that for the men whose family religious practices are destroyed, O Janardana, dwell in hell for an unknown period).

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम् | यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः
english: . Alas! We are involved in a great sin, in that we are prepared to kill our kinsmen, through greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.
brief_explanation: Alas, have we become prepared to commit great sin by being willing to kill our own kin for the greed of royal pleasure.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः | धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत्
english: . If the sons of Dhritarashtra with weapons in hand should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
brief_explanation: In this verse, it is suggested that if I (Krishna) am surrendered and unarmed, while the sons of Dhritarashtra are armed and prepared for battle, it would be more beneficial for me to let them engage in combat rather than participate myself.

speaker: Sanjaya
sanskrit: सञ्जय उवाच | एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः सङ्ख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् | विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः
english: . Sanjaya said Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna, casting away his bow and arrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot with his mind overwhelmed with sorrow.
brief_explanation: Arjuna, distressed with sorrow, casts away his bow and arrow on the seat of his chariot after Sri Krishna's first discourse in the Bhagavad Gita, known as The Yoga of Arjuna's Despondency.

speaker: Sanjaya
sanskrit: सञ्जय उवाच | तं तथा कृपयाविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम् | विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः
english: Sanjaya said To him who was thus overcome with pity and who was despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.
brief_explanation: Tam - to him Tatha - thus Kripaya - with pity Aavishstam - overcome Ashrupurnaakulakeshnam - with eyes filled with tears and agitated Visidantam - despondent Idam - this Vakyam - speech Uvacha - spoke Maghusoodanah - Madhusudana (Krishna)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम् | अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन
english: The Blessed Lord said Whence is this perilous strait come upon thee, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?
brief_explanation: Arjuna's dejection comes upon him in a perilous strait, seemingly unworthy (un-aryanlike), excluding heaven and being disgraceful.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते | क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप
english: Yield not to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit thee. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O scorcher of the foes!
brief_explanation: In Bhagavad Gita 2.3, Sage Sivananda explains that Partha (Arjuna) should not yield to impotence (klaib Yam), which can manifest as weakness of the heart (hRdaya daurbalyam). Instead, after abandoning it, he should stand up as a scorcher of foes (uttiShTha parantap).

speaker: Arjuna
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | कथं भीष्ममहं सङ्ख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन | इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन
english: Arjuna said How, O Madhusudana, shall I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are fit to be worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?
brief_explanation: Bhishma, I (Krishna) am counted among the warriors in battle. Drona and Madhusudana (another name for Krishna) will fight using arrows. Both are worthy to be worshipped as they are destroyers of enemies.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान् श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके | हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्
english: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I kill them, even in this world all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires will be stained with (their) blood.
brief_explanation: The term "Gurus" refers to teachers, and instead of killing, one should cultivate non-violence ("ahatva"). It is stated that these most noble Gurus are better than those who eat alms even in this world, having slain others for the sake of wealth. Moreover, it is indicated that the Gurus are also superior to those who enjoy material pleasures stained with blood.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः | यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्- तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः
english: I can hardly tell which will be better, that we should coner them or that they should coner us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, after slaying whom we do not wish to live, stand facing us.
brief_explanation: This verse discusses the dilemma of Arjuna, questioning if it is better for him or his enemies to conquer (yajema) in the battle, especially when considering that he does not wish to live after killing his relatives who are standing in the face of the Dhartarashtra clan.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेताः | यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्
english: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple. Instruct me who has taken refuge in Thee.
brief_explanation: This passage suggests a disciple asks the Lord, who has a mind confused about duty, whether good can be decisively known and if he should teach it to the disciple or the Lord should teach it to him, having taken refuge.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद् यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् | अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्
english: I do not see that it would remove this sorrow that burns up my senses, even if I should attain prosperous and unrivalled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.
brief_explanation: The passage does not provide a direct commentary, but it suggests that even with one's senses drying up due to grief, on earth, one can still achieve an unrivaled, prosperous dominion over gods and lordship, as nothing prevents this (from happening).

speaker: Sanjaya
sanskrit: सञ्जय उवाच | एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप | न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह
english: Sanjaya said Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha (the Lord of the senses), Arjuna (the coneror of sleep), the destroyer of foes, said to Krishna, "I will not fight" and became silent.
brief_explanation: Arjuna, also known as Gudakesha (conqueror of sleep) and Parantapa (destroyer of foes), remains silent after Hrishikesha (Lord Vishnu in his avatar as Krishna) speaks to him, choosing not to fight.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत | सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः
english: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, as if smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.
brief_explanation: Hrishikesha, speaking to Bharata, smiled as if and said this word to the despondent commander of both armies in the middle.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे | गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः
english: The Blessed Lord said Thou hast grieved for those that should not be grieved for, yet thou speakest words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.
brief_explanation: The verse introduces the philosophical foundation of the Gita. Bhishma and Drona, being eternal and virtuous, should not be grieved for. One who speaks words of wisdom yet grieves for the dead or living shows a lack of understanding about the immortal nature of the Self and the temporary nature of bodies.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः | न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्
english: Nor at any time indeed was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men, nor verily shall we ever cease to be hereafter.
brief_explanation: The passage discusses the eternal nature of the self, suggesting it persists across past, present, and future. It implies that despite the death of the physical body, there remains a form of life beyond.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा | तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति
english: Just as in this body the embodied (soul) passes into childhood, youth and old age, so also does it pass into another body; the firm man does not grieve thereat.
brief_explanation: The ego's passage in this body is continuous, similar to the transition from childhood to youth and from youth to old age. The Self does not die with the end of a stage such as childhood nor is born again at the start of another like youth. Just as the Self remains unchanged during these life stages, it also passes unaltered from one body to another.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः | आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत
english: The contacts of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which cause heat and cold, pleasure and pain, have a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.
brief_explanation: The passage discusses how sensory contacts with objects, such as cold or heat, can bring pleasure or pain, which are impermanent. These sensations originate from the Indriyas (senses) and are felt by the mind. It suggests that one should strive to endure these temporary sensations patiently, aiming for a balanced state of mind.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ | समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते
english: That firm man whom, surely, these afflict not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.
brief_explanation: The referred verse describes "Yam" as the one who identifies with the body, causing afflictions from pleasure and pain. "Ete" refer to individuals striving for immortality. The firm-minded individual ("Dhieram") who remains equal in pleasure and pain is fit for immortality.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः | उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः
english: The unreal hath no being; there is non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the Truth (or the seers of the Essence).
brief_explanation: The Atman (Self) is changeless and the only solid Reality, while the world of names and forms is ever-changing and thus unreal. The sage, through his intuition, directly cognizes the Self and perceives that the world vanishes like a mirage. He rejects names and forms, focusing on the underlying Essence (Satchidananda or Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् | विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति
english: Know that to be indestructible, by Which all this is pervaded. None can cause the destruction of That, the Imperishable.
brief_explanation: The Atman or Brahman, like ether, permeates all objects. Even if a pot breaks, the internal and external ether remains undestroyed. Similarly, though bodies and other objects may perish, the Atman or Self that pervades them cannot be destroyed.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः | अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत
english: These bodies of the embodied Self, Which is eternal, indestructible and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Arjuna.
brief_explanation: The bodies of the embodied, indestructible, immesaurable, and everlasting are said to have an end. Despite this, one should fight (yudhyasva), O Bharata, as Krishna removes Arjuna's delusion, grief, and despondency which arise from ignorance about the nature of the all-pervading Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् | उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते
english: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks It is slain, neither of them ï1knowsï1. It slays not, nor is It slain.
brief_explanation: The Self, as nondoer (Akarta), is neither the agent nor the object of slaying. One who thinks "I slay" or "I am slain" with the body or ego does not comprehend the true nature of the Self, which is indestructible and exists beyond the three periods of time. The body may undergo change and destruction, but the Self remains unaffected.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन् नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः | अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे
english: It is not born, nor does It ever die; after having been, It again ceases not to be; unborn, eternal, changeless and ancient, It is not killed when the body is killed.
brief_explanation: The Self is devoid of six types of transformations such as birth, existence, growth, transformation, decline, and death. Being indivisible, it neither diminishes nor grows, and remains eternal, changeless, and ancient. Birth and death only apply to the physical body; they do not affect the immortal Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम् | कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम्
english: Whosoever knows It to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and inexhaustible, how can that man slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?
brief_explanation: The enlightened sage, aware of the eternal, indestructible, unborn, and inexhaustible self, does not engage in killing or causing others to kill.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि | तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा- न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही
english: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so also the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others which are new.
brief_explanation: The text explains that just as a person sheds worn-out clothes and takes on new ones, similarly, a man casts off old bodies and enters into new ones. The embodied one undergoes such transformations.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः | न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः
english: Weapons cut It not, fire burns It not, water wets It not, wind dries It not.
brief_explanation: The Self, being indivisible and infinite, cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, wetted by water, or dried by wind as it is beyond such material effects.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च | नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः
english: This Self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted, nor dried up. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable and ancient.
brief_explanation: The Self is subtle, beyond the reach of speech and mind, difficult to understand. Lord Krishna describes the nature of the immortal Self in various ways to be grasped easily. The Self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or died.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते | तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि
english: This (Self) is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing This to be such, thou shouldst not grieve.
brief_explanation: The Self, unperceivable by physical eyes, is referred to as unmanifested (avyakta). As it can't be thought of through perception, it is considered unthinkable (acintya). Since the Self remains immutable in form, it is also described as unchangeable (avikarpya).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम् | तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि
english: But even if thou thinkest of It as being constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed, thou shouldst not grieve.
brief_explanation: The Lord, for argument's sake, accepts the common belief that the Self is continuously reborn with each new body and dies with each old one. Despite this, Arjuna should not grieve because birth is inevitable due to the nature of what is born being mortal, and death is inevitable due to what is born having an end. This is the unchanging law of nature.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च | तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि
english: For certain is death for the born, and certain is birth for the dead; therefore, over the inevitable thou shouldst not grieve.
brief_explanation: The text suggests that birth and death are both unavoidable. As a result, one ought not to grieve about something that is inevitable in life's cycle.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत | अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना
english: Beings are unmanifested in their beginning, manifested in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifested again in their end. What is there to grieve about?
brief_explanation: The physical body is visible only in its middle state, as it's a combination of the five elements that disintegrate after death and return to their source. Human relationships formed through attachment and delusion are similar to objects in a public inn, where they form and dissolve. In the same way, bodies do not exist in their purest forms (unmanifested) at the beginning or end, suggesting they may be illusory even in the middle state.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन- माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः | आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः शृणोति श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित्
english: One sees This (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of It as a wonder; another hears of It as a wonder; yet having heard, none understands It at all.
brief_explanation: This verse can be interpreted as follows: A person who perceives, listens to, and discusses the Self is considered amazing. Such individuals are scarce, being one in thousands. The Self is difficult to comprehend due to its profound nature.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत | तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि
english: This, the Indweller in the body of everyone, is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, thou shouldst not grieve for any creature.
brief_explanation: The indweller, which is indestructible and exists in all bodies, should not be grieved over because it is immune to destruction, regardless of whether it's in Bharata (the individual) or anyone else.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि | धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते
english: Further, having regard to thy duty, shouldst not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.
brief_explanation: The Lord offers worldly reasons for Arjuna to fight, having previously discussed the immortality of the Self and philosophical aspects. He suggests that fighting is a Kshatriya's own duty and a warrior should not waver from this. For a warrior, there is no higher pursuit than a righteous war.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम् | सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम्
english: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called upon to fight in such a battle that comes of itself as an open door to heaven.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests that a Kshatriya, O Partha, attains happiness and enters the opened gate of heaven by participating in such a righteous battle. This implies that death in a just war can lead to spiritual reward.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि | ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि
english: But if thou wilt not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned thine own duty and fame, thou shalt incur sin.
brief_explanation: The Lord encourages Arjuna, emphasizing potential loss of fame if he abstains from warfare. Arjuna earned renown by engaging with Lord Siva during their Kirata fight, receiving the Pasupatastra as a result.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम् | सम्भावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते
english: People, too, will recount thy everlasting dishonour; and to one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
brief_explanation: The commentary suggests that even after death, dishonor will be remembered in the world for a long time. Death, however, is considered preferable to disgrace for those who have achieved high status due to their valor and nobility.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः | येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम्
english: The great car-warriors will think that thou hast withdrawn from the battle through fear; and thou wilt be lightly held by them who have thought much of thee.
brief_explanation: Duryodhana and others may perceive you as having retreated from the battle due to fear, especially towards Karna. However, this perception is not accurate, as it's not due to compassion or reverence for elders and teachers. Those who have respected you for your chivalry will view your actions as a demonstration of lightness and possibly treat you with contempt.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून्वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः | निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम्
english: Thy enemies also, cavilling at thy power, will speak many abusive words. What is more painful than this?
brief_explanation: The passage suggests that the most unbearable and tormenting pain comes from being slandered, especially when one's words are improper or unfavorable. This form of criticism, or cavilling, exceeds any other form of pain in its intensity.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् | तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः
english: Slain, thou wilt obtain heaven; victorious, thou wilt enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.
brief_explanation: In this verse, Arjuna is told that he will obtain heaven if he conquers, or enjoy the earth if he dies in battle. Therefore, Arjuna is urged to stand up with a resolved mind for fight.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ | ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि
english: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, engage thou in battle for the sake of battle; thus thou shalt not incur sin.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests the practice of equanimity in actions, viewing pleasure, pain, gain, loss, victory, defeat, and other dualities equally during battle. If one engages in action with this attitude, they will not incur the fruits of their actions, leading to spiritual purification and freedom from the cycle of birth and death. This balance is achieved through persistent effort and vigilance.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: एषा तेऽभिहिता साङ्ख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु | बुद्ध्या युक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि
english: This, which has been taught to thee, is wisdon concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, thou shalt cast off the bonds of action.
brief_explanation: The Lord is teaching Arjuna the secret of Karma Yoga, a method to break free from the bondage of actions. This wisdom is presented in both Sankhya and Yoga philosophies. A practitioner of Karma Yoga performs duties without seeking personal gain or attachment, annihilating all pairs of opposites, and dedicates all works to the Lord, earning divine grace.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते | स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात्
english: In this there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm (production of contrary results or transgression). Even a little of this knowledge (even a little practice of this Yoga) protects one from great fear.
brief_explanation: In Karma Yoga, every action purifies the heart immediately, unlike religious ceremonies where uncompleted rituals result in fruit loss. Unlike agriculture or medicine, there's no uncertainty or harm in Karma Yoga, and even minor actions can save one from the fear of rebirth. Lord Krishna praises Karma Yoga to stimulate Arjuna's interest in this path of action.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन | बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम्
english: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is but a single one-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the irresolute.
brief_explanation: In the path to Bliss, there exists a single, resolute thought of determination. This single-minded focus arises from right knowledge. The yogi gathers and concentrates all dissipated thoughts through discrimination and dispassion, eliminating mental wavering or vacillation.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः | वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः
english: Flowery speech is uttered by the unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogising words of the Vedas, O Arjuna, saying, "There is nothing else."
brief_explanation: The unwise, enamored by the Vedas' ritualistic portion (Karma Kanda), emphasize specific actions for specific rewards, focusing on heavenly pleasures. They claim there is nothing beyond these sensual enjoyments. The Jnana Kanda, dealing with knowledge, includes the Aranyakas and Upanishads, which discuss the Supreme Self, but the Mimamsakas, who focus on rituals, prioritize transient life in heaven over liberation through knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम् | क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति
english: Full of desires, having heaven as their goal, (they utter speech which is directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods abounding in specific actions, for the attainment of pleasure and power.
brief_explanation: Desire-driven individuals aiming for heaven, motivated by their works to reincarnate, and pursuing pleasures and power through specific actions.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम् | व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते
english: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teaching, ï1thatï1 determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and Samadhi (superconscious state).
brief_explanation: The individuals fixated on pleasure and power lack mental stability, unable to focus or meditate due to constant planning for material acquisition. Their minds are perpetually restless, and they lack a steady, poised understanding.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन | निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान्
english: The Vedas deal with the three attributes (of Nature); be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites, and ever remain in the ality of Sattva (goodness), freed from (the thought of) acisition and preservation, and be established in the Self.
brief_explanation: The verse 2.45 refers to states dealing with the three attributes or gunas: Sattva (purity, light, harmony), Rajas (passion, motion), and Tamas (darkness, inertia). It also mentions being free from the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, gain and loss. The individual should be established in the Self, free from the thought of acquisition and preservation for peace of mind and concentration on the Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः सम्प्लुतोदके | तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः
english: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as is a reservoir of water in a place where there is a flood.
brief_explanation: The passage suggests that for a sage who has realized the Self, the Vedas offer no new knowledge as they possess infinite self-knowledge already. However, this does not imply that the Vedas are useless. They provide transient pleasures and spiritual guidance to those starting on the spiritual path, and their enjoined actions lead to bliss when subsumed by Self-knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन | मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि
english: Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits; let not the fruits of action be thy motive, nor let thy attachment be to inaction.
brief_explanation: The explanation for verse 2.47 is: 1. Perform actions without seeking the fruits, under any circumstances, as it prevents rebirth and brings purification of heart. 2.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय | सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते
english: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure. Evenness of mind is called Yoga.
brief_explanation: The text "Yogasthah kuru karmaani sangam tyaktva dhananjaya" implies that one should perform actions while being steadfast in Yoga, detached from the results, O Dhananjaya. This equanimity of mind, or samatvam, is called Yoga (III.14, IV.20 referenced). The attainment of Self-knowledge through actions without desire for fruit is success (Siddhi), while expecting fruits leads to failure.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय | बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः
english: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdon is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are they whose motive is the fruit.
brief_explanation: Action aligned with equanimity is the Yoga of wisdom, where the practitioner remains unaffected by success or failure. They do not pursue rewards for their actions. Their reason is grounded in Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते | तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्
english: Endowed with wisdom (evenness of mind), one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote thyself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.
brief_explanation: Work performed for fruits binds a person, bringing new life to enjoy them. However, work done with an even mind (wisdom-based yoga) does not bind, as it is no action when the mind unites with the Lord and attributes actions to the Divine Actor within.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः | जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम्
english: The wise, possessed of knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the fetters of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests that those who perform actions for God, without seeking personal gain, are freed from the cycle of birth and attain an immortal abode beyond evil. Sages with even minds abandon the fruits of their actions, escaping both good and bad actions. The wisdom referred to in verses 49-51 could be Atmajnana, or Self-knowledge, achieved through purification by Karma Yoga.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति | तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च
english: When thy intellect crosses beyond the mire of delusion, then thou shalt attain to indifference as to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.
brief_explanation: The mire of delusion refers to the confusion between self and non-self. When one's mind becomes pure, they will achieve indifference towards things heard or yet to be heard, regarding them as useless and developing disgust. (Cf.XVI.24)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला | समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि
english: When thy intellect, which is perplexed by the Veda text, which thou hast read, shall stand immovable and steady in the Self, then thou shalt attain Self-realisation.
brief_explanation: The intellect becomes steadfast and immune to doubt when it is firmly rooted in the Self, transcending the confusion between the paths of action and renunciation. At this point, one achieves Self-realization or knowledge of the Self.

speaker: Arjuna
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव | स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम्
english: Arjuna said What, O Krishna, is the description of him who has steady wisdom, and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how does he sit, how does he walk?
brief_explanation: The characteristic marks of one in Samadhi, a superconscious state, are described. These include the manner of speaking, sitting, and moving about. Steady wisdom, or settled knowledge of one's identity with Brahman, is achieved through direct realization.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | प्रजहाति यदा कामान्सर्वान्पार्थ मनोगतान् | आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते
english: The Blessed Lord said When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then is he said to be one of steady wisdom.
brief_explanation: When one becomes satisfied and attains supreme bliss in the Self, they no longer crave for sensual pleasures, considering all worldly desires as insignificant. This is the case for a sage with steady wisdom, as described in the verse.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः | वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते
english: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not hanker after pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
brief_explanation: The sage of steady wisdom, as described by Lord Krishna, remains undisturbed in adversity and unshaken in pleasure. He is free from attachment, fear, anger, and hankering for sensual pleasures. This individual is called a sage.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम् | नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता
english: He who is everywhere without attachment, on meeting with anything good or bad, who neither rejoices not hastes, his wisdom is fixed.
brief_explanation: The sage, rooted in the Self, remains indifferent to both pleasure and pain. He is detached from life and body, identifying with the Supreme Self (Brahman). He neither praises nor censures others due to his poised understanding or evenness of mind.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः | इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता
english: When, like the tortoise which withdraws on all sides its limbs, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.
brief_explanation: The Yogi, through Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses), steadies his wisdom, allowing it to focus internally rather than being distracted by the external world. This power enables the Yogi to enter Samadhi in any setting, even amidst noise and chaos, as if they are unperturbed by the outside world. The Yogi's senses become his obedient servants, easily controlled at will.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः | रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते
english: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man leaving the longing (behind); but his longing also turns away on seeing the Supreme.
brief_explanation: The knowledge of the Self can eliminate all latent tendencies and subtle desires, including attachments to sensory objects. However, even after abstaining from sensual objects, an individual may still have a lingering taste or longing for them.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः | इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः
english: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, do violently carry away the mind of a wise man though he be striving (to control them).
brief_explanation: The passage suggests that a person should control their turbulent senses to prevent being distracted from reaching spiritual destinations like Param Dhama, eternal peace, or final liberation. This is compared to controlling horses on a journey.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः | वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता
english: Having restrained them all he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.
brief_explanation: The Yogi should control all their senses, sit with focus on the Supreme Me, and maintain a calm mind. This Yogi, whose wisdom is settled, has subjugated his senses and is established in the Self. According to Sri Sankaracharya, Asita Matparah means he should contemplate that I am no other than him.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते | सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते
english: When a man thinks of the objects, attachment for them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger arises.
brief_explanation: The thinking on sense objects leads to attachment, which spawns a desire to possess them. This desire then gives birth to anger when attempts to obtain them are thwarted. If anyone hinders the acquisition, there is a development of hatred, fighting, and hostility.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः | स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति
english: From anger comes delusion; from delusion loss of memory; from loss of memory the destruction of discrimination; from the destruction of discrimination he perishes.
brief_explanation: Anger leads to delusion, causing loss of memory and rationality. Without discrimination, a person acts impulsively, speaking and doing things without regard for right or wrong, leading eventually to their own destruction.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: रागद्वेषविमुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन् | (or वियुक्तैस्तु) आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति
english: But the self-controlled man, moving among the objects with the senses under restraint and free from attraction and repulsion, attains to peace.
brief_explanation: The disciplined person moves among sense objects with self-restraint, free from attraction and repulsion, attaining peace by mastering the mind and senses according to their will, only taking necessary items and avoiding forbidden ones, in response to Arjuna's fourth question about a sage's movement (referenced in III.7.19-25 and XVIII.9).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते | प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते
english: In that peace all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranil-minded soon becomes steady.
brief_explanation: The Arrival of peace, freedom from all pains, and destruction of suffering happens within the tranquil-minded yogi soon. His intellect becomes steadfast, rooted in the Self, implying mastery over reason.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना | न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम्
english: There is no knowledge of the Self to the unsteady and to the unsteady no meditation is possible, and to the unmeditative there can be no peace, and to the man who has no peace, how can there be happiness?
brief_explanation: The unsteady individual cannot attain knowledge of the Self or achieve peace through meditation, as they are constantly distracted by desires for sense objects. Without meditation and self-control, it is impossible to find inner peace and happiness.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते | तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि
english: For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind (carries away) a boat on the waters.
brief_explanation: The mind following the senses, constantly engaging with sensual objects, undermines one's ability for discrimination. Like a boat carried off course by the wind, the mind diverts the aspirant from their spiritual journey and steers them towards worldly senses.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः | इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता
english: Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense-objects.
brief_explanation: The commentary suggests that when one successfully restrains their senses from being drawn towards sense objects, their mind ceases to wander and knowledge becomes steady, resembling a stable lamp. This state indicates the Yogi's establishment in the Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी | यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः
english: That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the Muni (sage) who sees.
brief_explanation: In this verse, the ordinary man perceives the world as day (waking state), while it's considered illusion for the sage. The sage lives in the Self (spiritual awakening) and sees the worldly phenomena as night. Conversely, the world is a nonentity for the sage, but life in spirit is night for the ordinary man who experiences sensual enjoyment.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् | तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी
english: He attains peace into whom all desires enter as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires.
brief_explanation: The ocean, filled from all sides with water yet unmoved, symbolizes the sage who remains unaffected by entering desires from all directions, as he resides in his own Self. The desirer of sensual enjoyment and multiple desires does not attain peace or liberation. (Cf.XVIII.53-54)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान्पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः | निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति
english: That man attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of mine and without egoism.
brief_explanation: The man who abandons all desires, renounces his sense of self and possessions, and is indifferent to even basic needs, attains eternal peace. This description resembles the state of Moksha mentioned in Chapter 2, Verse 55.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति | स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति
english: This is the Brahmic seat (eternal state), O son of Pritha. Attaining to this, none is deluded. Being established therein, even at the end of life, one attains to oneness with Brahman.
brief_explanation: The Brahmic state, described as renouncing everything and living in Brahman, is attained when one obtains this state and remains undeluded. Even at the end of life, if one stays in this state, they achieve Moksha. If someone maintains this state throughout their life, they attain BrahmaNirvana.

speaker: Arjuna
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | ज्यायसी चेत्कर्मणस्ते मता बुद्धिर्जनार्दन | तत्किं कर्मणि घोरे मां नियोजयसि केशव
english: Arjuna said If Thou thinkest that knowledge is superior to action, O Krishna, why then, O Kesava, dost Thou ask me to engage in this terrible action?
brief_explanation: The superiority of action is discussed, with the question raised if this thought (mata) is Your knowledge (buddhi). Janardana (a name for Krishna) then states 'then why do You engage in action (karmani), terrible as it may be (ghore), and engage Me (mam) Kesava?' This exchange occurs in verses 49, 50, and 51 of Chapter II.

speaker: Unknown
sanskrit: व्यामिश्रेणेव वाक्येन बुद्धिं मोहयसीव मे | तदेकं वद निश्चित्य येन श्रेयोऽहमाप्नुयाम्
english: With this apparently perplexing speech, Thou confusest, as it were, my understanding; therefore tell me that one way for certain by which I may attain bliss.
brief_explanation: The student, Arjuna, seeks clarity from Lord Krishna on whether he should pursue knowledge or action for attaining the supreme bliss or liberation. (Reference: V.1)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | लोकेऽस्मिन् द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ | ज्ञानयोगेन साङ्ख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम्
english: The Blessed Lord said In this world there is a twofold path, as I said before, O sinless one; the path of knowledge of the Sankhyas and the path of action of the Yogins.
brief_explanation: In this world, the twofold paths - Knowledge (Jnana Yoga) and Action (Karma Yoga) - were described by Lord Krishna in different sections of the Bhagavad Gita. The path of knowledge was explained in chapters II verses 11-38, while the path of action was discussed from verses 40 to 53. These paths are suitable for those with specific characteristics: sharp intellect and subtle understanding for Jnana Yoga, and a tendency for work for Karma Yoga.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते | न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति
english: Not by non-performance of actions does man reach actionlessness; nor by mere renunciation does he attain to perfection.
brief_explanation: The terms actionlessness (Naishkarmyam) and perfection (Siddhi) are interchangeable. A sage who has attained perfection or reached a state of actionlessness is in his inherent nature as Existence, Knowledge, Bliss Absolute (Satchidananda Svarupa). This sage has no compulsion or desire for actions as a means to an end; instead, they find complete satisfaction in the Self.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न हि कश्चित्क्षणमपि जातु तिष्ठत्यकर्मकृत् | कार्यते ह्यवशः कर्म सर्वः प्रकृतिजैर्गुणैः
english: Verily none can ever remain for even a moment without performing action; for everyone is made to act helplessly indeed by the alities born of Nature.
brief_explanation: The Gunas (alities of Nature) are Sattva (harmony, light, purity), Rajas (passion, motion), and Tamas (inertia, darkness). Sattvic actions aid in attaining Moksha, while Rajasic and Tamasic actions bind one to Samsara. The enlightened individual who knows the Self has transcended these alities, becoming a Gunatita.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन् | इन्द्रियार्थान्विमूढात्मा मिथ्याचारः स उच्यते
english: He who, restraining the organs of action, sits thinking of the sense-objects in mind, he of deluded understanding is called a hypocrite.
brief_explanation: The five organs of action, Karma Indriyas, are Vak (speech), Pani (hands), Padam (feet), Upastha (genitals), and Guda (anus). They originate from the Rajasic portion of the five subtle elements - Vak from Akasa Tanmatra (ether), Pani from Vayu Tanmatra (air), Padam from Agni Tanmatra (fire), Upastha from Apas Tanmatra (water), and Guda from Prithivi Tanmatra (earth). A person who controls these organs of action, revolving in his mind thoughts about sense objects, is deluded and a hypocrite.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यस्त्विन्द्रियाणि मनसा नियम्यारभतेऽर्जुन | कर्मेन्द्रियैः कर्मयोगमसक्तः स विशिष्यते
english: But whosoever, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, engages himself in Karma Yoga with the organs of action, without attachment, he excels.
brief_explanation: The individual who controls their senses with the mind, performing actions using their organs of action without attachment to results or egoism, is considered superior to one who acts out of hypocrisy or false conduct. The five organs of knowledge include the eyes, ears, nose, skin, and tongue. (Cf.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः | शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः
english: Do thou perform (thy) bounden duty, for action is superior to inaction and even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for thee by inaction.
brief_explanation: Niyatam Karma refers to duties that are obligatory and bound to be performed. Neglecting these duties results in demerit. Performing them does not lead to specific rewards or merits.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः | तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर
english: The world is bound by actions other than those performed for the sake of sacrifice; do thou, therefore, O son of Kunti (Arjuna), perform action for that sake (for sacrifice alone), free from attachment.
brief_explanation: Yajna refers to sacrifice, religious rites, or unselfish actions with pure motives, or even God (Vishnu). Performing actions for the Lord purifies one's heart and frees them from action-boundedness. When selflessness does not guide an action, it leads to continued existence in Samsara, regardless of its goodness or glory.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: सहयज्ञाः प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा पुरोवाच प्रजापतिः | अनेन प्रसविष्यध्वमेष वोऽस्त्विष्टकामधुक्
english: The Creator, having in the beginning (of creation) created mankind together with sacrifice, said, "By this shall ye propagate; let this be the milch cow of your desires (the cow which yields all the desired objects)."
brief_explanation: Prajapati, the Creator, spoke to mankind in the beginning, stating that by this (the path of righteousness and selfless action), they shall propagate. This path is likened to a "milch cow of desires" (Ishktakamadhuk) which fulfills all one's wishes, similar to Kamadhenu from Indra's mythology.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: देवान्भावयतानेन ते देवा भावयन्तु वः | परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ
english: With this do ye nourish the gods and may those gods nourish you; thus nourishing one another, ye shall attain to the highest good.
brief_explanation: This verse refers to the gods as the shining ones, who are nourished by the sacrifice. In return, they provide benefits such as rain, with the ultimate goal being the attainment of the highest good - either liberation from the cycle of birth and death or attainment of heaven, depending on the aspirant's motive.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: इष्टान्भोगान्हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः | तैर्दत्तानप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः
english: The gods, nourished by the sacrifice, will give you the desired objects. So, he who enjoys the objects given by the gods without offering (in return) to them, is verily a thief.
brief_explanation: The text suggests that if one is nourished by sacrifices made to the gods, they will be given desired objects such as children, cattle, and property. Conversely, one who enjoys what has been given by the gods without offering anything in return is likened to a thief or a dacoit of the gods' property.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः | भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात्
english: The righteous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are freed from all sins; but those sinful ones who cook food (only) for their own sake verily eat sin.
brief_explanation: Those who eat the remnants of food from the five places after performing the five great sacrifices (DevaYajna, BrahmaYajna/RishiYajna, PitriYajna, NriYajna, BhutaYajna) are freed from all sins. This is because these sins are washed away by the performance of the five MahaYajnas or great sacrifices that every Dvija (twice-born or first three castes in Hindu society, especially Brahmins) ought to perform.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः | यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यो यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः
english: From food come forth beings; from rain food is produced; from sacrifice arises rain and sacrifice is born of action.
brief_explanation: The text describes that beings come from food, rain is produced by the process of food creation, and both rain and sacrifice arise from action. In this context, Yajna refers to Apurva or the unseen form of a sacrifice before its fruit becomes visible.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कर्म ब्रह्मोद्भवं विद्धि ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम् | तस्मात्सर्वगतं ब्रह्म नित्यं यज्ञे प्रतिष्ठितम्
english: Know thou that action comes from Brahma and Brahma comes from the Imperishable. Therefore, the all-pervading (Brahma) ever rests in sacrifice.
brief_explanation: Karma is considered as arising from Brahma, which may refer to the Veda. Just as breath comes from a man, so does the Veda come from the Imperishable or Omniscient. The Veda is established in sacrifice, primarily dealing with sacrifices and their performance (Cf.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः | अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति
english: He who does not follow here the wheel thus set revolving, who is of sinful life, rejoicing in the senses, he lives in vain, O Arjuna.
brief_explanation: The wheel of action, based on Vedas and sacrifice, is set in motion by the Creator. One who does not follow this by studying Vedas and performing sacrifices, but indulges in sensual pleasures, lives in vain and wastes their life. Living against this law is committing sin, violating the Creator's law being the worst offense.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यस्त्वात्मरतिरेव स्यादात्मतृप्तश्च मानवः | आत्मन्येव च सन्तुष्टस्तस्य कार्यं न विद्यते
english: But for that man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self and who is content in the Self alone, verily there is nothing to do.
brief_explanation: The man who rejoices in the Self, is satisfied and contented within his own Self, does not have work to be done as for him, there is nothing left to do since he has already fulfilled all actions and desires, attaining complete satisfaction. (Cf. II.55)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: नैव तस्य कृतेनार्थो नाकृतेनेह कश्चन | न चास्य सर्वभूतेषु कश्चिदर्थव्यपाश्रयः
english: For him there is no interest whatever in what is done or what is not done; nor does he depend on any being for any object.
brief_explanation: The sage, who rejoices in the Self, gains nothing through actions and is unaffected by inaction (regarding Pratyavaya Dosha). He doesn't rely on others for obtaining any specific object, thus needing no exertion or favor from them.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर | असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः
english: Therefore without attachment, do thou always perform action which should be done; for by performing action without attachment man reaches the Supreme.
brief_explanation: Performing actions without attachment and for the sake of the Supreme leads to self-realization, as the pure heart brings one closer to the Lord. (Refer II.64, IV.19-23, XVIII.49)

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः | लोकसंग्रहमेवापि सम्पश्यन्कर्तुमर्हसि
english: Janaka and others attained perfection verily by action only; even with a view to the protection of the masses thou shouldst perform action.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests that even those who have attained perfection, like Janaka and others, continue to perform actions for the sake of the masses, serving as examples and offering guidance.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः | स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते
english: Whatsoever a great man does, that the other men also do; whatever he sets up as the standard, that the world (mankind) follows.
brief_explanation: Great men set societal standards as they are imitated by others who view them as their moral superiors. The actions of the best among us are seen as authoritative, and people strive to emulate them.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न मे पार्थास्ति कर्तव्यं त्रिषु लोकेषु किञ्चन | नानवाप्तमवाप्तव्यं वर्त एव च कर्मणि
english: There is nothing in the three worlds, O Arjuna, that should be done by Me, nor is there anything unattained that should be attained; yet I engage Myself in action.
brief_explanation: The text explains that as the Lord of the universe, God has no personal need to engage in action, yet He does so. The reason for this is to set an example for others, especially leaders, to encourage them to follow a noble path and guide the masses away from wrongdoing.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यदि ह्यहं न वर्तेयं जातु कर्मण्यतन्द्रितः | मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः
english: For, should I not ever engage Myself in action, unwearied, men would in every way follow My path, O Arjuna.
brief_explanation: If I, Krishna, remain inactive, men will follow My path unweariedly and thus fall into a state of inertia (Tamas). This applies to all people, O Partha.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: उत्सीदेयुरिमे लोका न कुर्यां कर्म चेदहम् | सङ्करस्य च कर्ता स्यामुपहन्यामिमाः प्रजाः
english: These worlds would perish if I did not perform action; I should be the author of confusion of castes and destruction of these beings.
brief_explanation: Engaging in action is necessary, as inaction by people could lead to a lack of duty fulfillment and confusion in castes. If such confusion arises, the author (you) would have to destroy the beings (people).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत | कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्चिकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम्
english: As the ignorant men act from attachment to action, O Bharata (Arjuna), so should the wise act without attachment, wishing the welfare of the world.
brief_explanation: The ignorant perform actions with expectation of rewards, while the wise act selflessly for the betterment of the world. The wise, knowing their true nature, do not act for personal gain but to inspire others towards peace, harmony, and spiritual growth.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: न बुद्धिभेदं जनयेदज्ञानां कर्मसङ्गिनाम् | जोषयेत्सर्वकर्माणि विद्वान्युक्तः समाचरन्
english: Let no wise man unsettle the mind of ignorant people who are attached to action; he should engage them in all actions, himself fulfilling them with devotion.
brief_explanation: The ignorant may believe in doing actions for personal enjoyment, but a wise person should not unsettle this belief. Instead, they should diligently perform their duties without attachment, setting an example for others. The wise may also persuade the ignorant to fulfill their duties and highlight the rewards of selfless service both here and in the afterlife, gradually sowing seeds of Karma Yoga (selfless service) in them.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: प्रकृतेः क्रियमाणानि गुणैः कर्माणि सर्वशः | अहङ्कारविमूढात्मा कर्ताहमिति मन्यते
english: All actions are wrought in all cases by the alities of Nature only. He whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
brief_explanation: The term "Prakriti" refers to nature, which is a state where the three Gunas - Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas - exist in equilibrium. When this balance is disturbed, creation occurs, resulting in the formation of body, senses, and mind. A person deluded by egoism mistakenly identifies the Self with these manifestations and believes 'I am the doer.' However, in reality, it's the Gunas that perform all actions (as suggested in verses III.29, V.9, IX.9-10, X.9-10, Xiii.21-24, 30-32, XVIII.13-14).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: तत्त्ववित्तु महाबाहो गुणकर्मविभागयोः | गुणा गुणेषु वर्तन्त इति मत्वा न सज्जते
english: But he who knows the Truth, O mighty-armed (Arjuna), about the divisions of the alities and (their) functions, knowing that the Gunas as senses move amidst the Gunas as the sense-objects, is not attached.
brief_explanation: The knower of Truth, understanding the distinction between the Self and the three Gunas' functions, recognizes that the alities as sense organs operate among sense objects. This understanding leads to detachment from actions, implying a recognition of non-doership.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: प्रकृतेर्गुणसम्मूढाः सज्जन्ते गुणकर्मसु | तानकृत्स्नविदो मन्दान्कृत्स्नविन्न विचालयेत्
english: Those deluded by the alities of Nature are attached to the functions of the alities. The man of perfect knowledge should not unsettle the foolish one who is of imperfect knowledge.
brief_explanation: The ignorant, deluded by Gunas (natural tendencies), are attached to actions driven by imperfect knowledge. The wise, with perfect knowledge, should not disrupt the faith of such individuals as it may lead to inertia or an idle life. Instead, the wise should initially encourage them to perform Sakama actions (actions for fruit) and gradually guide them towards Karma Yoga (selfless action), promoting heart purification and Self-realization.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: मयि सर्वाणि कर्माणि संन्यस्याध्यात्मचेतसा | निराशीर्निर्ममो भूत्वा युध्यस्व विगतज्वरः
english: Renouncing all actions in Me, with the mind centred in the Self, free from hope and egoism, and from (mental) fever, do thou fight.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests that one should relinquish all actions to God, considering Him as the doer. It implies that actions are performed by God for His own purpose. The practitioner should be free from desire and ego, centered in the Self, devoid of hope and sorrow (free from mental fever).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: ये मे मतमिदं नित्यमनुतिष्ठन्ति मानवाः | श्रद्धावन्तोऽनसूयन्तो मुच्यन्ते तेऽपि कर्मभिः
english: Those men who constantly practise this teaching of Mine with faith and without cavilling, they too are freed from actions.
brief_explanation: The individuals who constantly practice this teaching, filled with faith and free from cavilling (doubting or complaining), are freed from actions. These individuals, including those as well, are liberated by their actions. Faith in the Self, scriptures, and spiritual teacher's teachings is a mental attitude composed of higher emotions such as faith, reverence, and humility.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: ये त्वेतदभ्यसूयन्तो नानुतिष्ठन्ति मे मतम् | सर्वज्ञानविमूढांस्तान्विद्धि नष्टानचेतसः
english: But those who carp at My teaching and do not practise it, deluded of all knowledge, and devoid of discrimination, know them to be doomed to destruction.
brief_explanation: The individuals who are stubborn, criticize the Lord's teachings, and don't follow them, are inevitably headed for ruin as they lack discrimination and are deluded of all knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि | प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि निग्रहः किं करिष्यति
english: Even a wise man acts in accordance with his own nature; beings will follow Nature; what can restraint do?
brief_explanation: The verse indicates that a wise man can conform to his own nature while also exerting restraint over it, causing beings to follow him. However, this concept suggests no scope for personal exertion is incorrect. A seeker of truth who practices meditation and has control over the four means (Yoga's eight limbs) can master Nature, even though the ignorant man succumbs to natural propensities like love and hatred.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: इन्द्रियस्येन्द्रियस्यार्थे रागद्वेषौ व्यवस्थितौ | तयोर्न वशमागच्छेत्तौ ह्यस्य परिपन्थिनौ
english: Attachment and aversion for the objects of the senses abide in the senses; let none come under their sway; for, they are his foes.
brief_explanation: The senses have attraction for pleasant objects (raga) and aversion for unpleasant ones (dvesha). Controlling these two currents, attachment and aversion, allows one to avoid their sway, enabling personal exertion or Purushartha. Nature, drawing one through these currents, can be controlled with discrimination and Vichara, leading to immortality and eternal bliss.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् | स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः
english: Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit than the duty of another well discharged. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is fraught with fear (is productive of danger).
brief_explanation: The text suggests that it's preferable for an individual to fulfill their own duty, even if it lacks merit, rather than performing another's duty perfectly. Performing another's duty comes with risks, while adhering to one's own duty, though it may lead to death, guarantees a heavenly destination. Arjuna, as a Kshatriya, should fight in righteous battles, and not renounce his duty or take up another's duty.

speaker: Arjuna
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः | अनिच्छन्नपि वार्ष्णेय बलादिव नियोजितः
english: Arjuna said But impelled by what does man commit sin, though against his wishes, O Varshneya (Krishna), constrained as it were, by force?
brief_explanation: Varshneya refers to someone born into the Vrishni clan, which was Krishna's family. In this context, it implies Krishna himself. The verse suggests that even though Krishna, as a man and not wishing for it, is impelled or constrained by some force (possibly divine duty) to bring about sin in others.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | काम एष क्रोध एष रजोगुणसमुद्भवः | महाशनो महापाप्मा विद्ध्येनमिह वैरिणम्
english: The Blessed Lord said It is desire, it is anger both of the ality of Rajas, all-devouring, all-sinful; know this as the foe here (in this world).
brief_explanation: Desire and anger originate from the attribute of Rajas, making them all-devouring and sinful. Recognize them as your foes in this world, as they hinder your spiritual progress (similar to XVI.21). The Lord possesses six attributes: knowledge, dispassion, fame, divine manifestations, wealth, and might, but desire is the root of all wrong actions.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: धूमेनाव्रियते वह्निर्यथादर्शो मलेन च | यथोल्बेनावृतो गर्भस्तथा तेनेदमावृतम्
english: As fire is enveloped by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo by the amnion, so is this enveloped by that.
brief_explanation: The verse describes three analogies: the universe, knowledge, and desire. It compares them to a mirror covered by dust, fire enveloped by smoke, and an embryo covered by the amnion. Thus, it signifies that these entities are enveloped or influenced by something else (dust, smoke, amnion).

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: आवृतं ज्ञानमेतेन ज्ञानिनो नित्यवैरिणा | कामरूपेण कौन्तेय दुष्पूरेणानलेन च
english: O Arjuna, wisdom is enveloped by this constant enemy of the wise in the form of desire, which is unappeasable as fire.
brief_explanation: Desire, enveloped by the wise, remains unappeasable like fire by fire. No matter how many objects one possesses, they cannot satisfy desire. The wise understand that desire brings only trouble and misery, making it a constant enemy for them, while the ignorant consider it as a friend due to their cravings.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: इन्द्रियाणि मनो बुद्धिरस्याधिष्ठानमुच्यते | एतैर्विमोहयत्येष ज्ञानमावृत्य देहिनम्
english: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied by veiling his wisdom.
brief_explanation: The senses, mind, and intellect are referred to as the seat or abode where delusion resides, enveloping wisdom in the embodied one. Lord Krishna identifies this abode of desire for Arjuna, allowing him to easily combat and eliminate it.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: तस्मात्त्वमिन्द्रियाण्यादौ नियम्य भरतर्षभ | पाप्मानं प्रजहि ह्येनं ज्ञानविज्ञाननाशनम्
english: Therefore, O best of the Bharatas (Arjuna), controlling the senses first, do thou kill this sinful thing, the destroyer of knowledge and realisation.
brief_explanation: The verse suggests that one should control the senses to destroy the sinful nature of ignorance (ignorance being both indirect knowledge and personal experience). This refers to eliminating both knowledge obtained from scriptures and personal realization for spiritual progress.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः | मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः
english: They say that the senses are superior (to the body); superior to the senses is the mind; superior to the mind is the intellect; one who is superior even to the intellect is He (the Self).
brief_explanation: The senses are more subtle and internal than the gross, external body. The mind performs the functions of the five senses, making it superior to them. The intellect has the faculty of discrimination, and when the mind doubts, the intellect comes to its rescue.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: एवं बुद्धेः परं बुद्ध्वा संस्तभ्यात्मानमात्मना | जहि शत्रुं महाबाहो कामरूपं दुरासदम्
english: Thus knowing Him Who is superior to the intellect and restraining the self by the Self, slay thou, O mighty-armed Arjuna, the enemy in the form of desire, hard to coner.
brief_explanation: In this passage, the text suggests that one should restrain the lower self by the higher Self and subdue the lower mind by the higher mind to conquer desire, which is difficult due to its complex nature but not impossible with constant practice and increased Sattvic ality. The dialogue between Sri Krishna and Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita concludes the third discourse on the Yoga of Action.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम् | विवस्वान्मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत्
english: The Blessed Lord said I taught this imperishable Yoga to Vivasvan; he told it to Manu; Manu proclaimed it to Ikshvaku.
brief_explanation: Vivasvan, meaning the sun, was taught this imperishable Yoga by Ikshvaku, a descendant of Manu. This yoga's result, Moksha, is imperishable. By knowing this Yoga, rulers can protect Brahmanas and rule justly.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: एवं परम्पराप्राप्तमिमं राजर्षयो विदुः | स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप
english: This, handed down thus in regular succession, the royal sages knew. This Yoga, by long lapse of time, has been lost here, O Parantapa (burner of the foes).
brief_explanation: Royal sages, who were also kings, learned this Yoga in succession. Over long periods of time, this Yoga was destroyed, and Arjuna, known as Parantapa, could burn or harass his foes like the sun with his valour and power.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: स एवायं मया तेऽद्य योगः प्रोक्तः पुरातनः | भक्तोऽसि मे सखा चेति रहस्यं ह्येतदुत्तमम्
english: That same ancient Yoga has been today taught to thee by Me, for thou art My devotee and My friend; it is the supreme secret.
brief_explanation: The Yoga taught here is a profound and subtle secret, revealing the supreme truth by the Lord to his friend and devotee.

speaker: Arjuna
sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः | कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति
english: Arjuna said Later on was Thy birth, and prior to it was the birth of Vivasvan (the Sun); how am I to understand that Thou taughtest this Yoga in the beginning?
brief_explanation: In the beginning, Vivasvan was born earlier in the process of evolution, while your birth occurred later as Vasudeva. The inconsistency arises because Krishna, as an eternal being, does not have a birth or death. Instead, it is explained that He imparted the Yoga knowledge to Vivasvan and now to you, but not in the linear sense of a temporal sequence.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन | तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप
english: The Blessed Lord said Many births of Mine have passed as well as of thine, O Arjuna; I know them all but thou knowest not, O Parantapa (scorcher of foes).
brief_explanation: Arjuna lacks intuitional knowledge about his past lives due to his previous actions, while Krishna (referred to as Parantapa) has omniscience and knows all of Arjuna's past lives.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन् | प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय सम्भवाम्यात्ममायया
english: Though I am unborn, of imperishable nature, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet, governing My own Nature, I am born by My own Maya.
brief_explanation: The Lord, being imperishable, governs over Nature which is responsible for beings coming into existence through His own Maya (illusory power). While man is deluded by the three qualities of Nature, the Lord's control over Maya means He is not subject to them, appearing to be born and embodied but maintaining a divine nature unaffected in reality. (Cf.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत | अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम्
english: Whenever there is decline of righteousness, O Arjuna, and rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself.
brief_explanation: Whenever there's a decline of righteousness, and rise of unrighteousness among the people of Bharata, I manifest Myself. The term 'Dharma' refers to that which sustains and supports, aiding a person towards salvation. On the other hand, 'Adharma' represents that which leads to irreligion or unrighteousness, pulling a person away from spiritual elevation.

speaker: Krishna
sanskrit: परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् | धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे
english: For the protection of the good, for the destruction of the wicked and for the establishment of righteousness, I am born in every age.
brief_explanation: The passage refers to four purposes of Vishnu's descent: protection of righteous people, destruction of evildoers, establishment of righteousness, and being born in every age. Righteous people are those who serve humanity, are selfless, and devote their lives to divine contemplation. Evil doers, on the other hand, break societal laws, commit atrocious crimes, and act unrighteously.

speaker: Krishna
